title: Sundew and the Ghosts
summary: In the village of Skruväng, deep in the forests of Småland, there lived a girl named Sundew—called sårfot in the old tongue because her grandmother said she was as delicate and as keen as the tiny carnivorous plant that grew in the boggy meadows.
full_text:
In the village of Skruväng, deep in the forests of Småland, there lived a girl named Sundew—called sårfot in the old tongue because her grandmother said she was as delicate and as keen as the tiny carnivorous plant that grew in the boggy meadows. What made Sundew truly different was not her name or her gentle nature, but her sight. From the time she was a small child, she could see what others could not—the spirits of the dead who walked the mists of twilight.

The village folk were uneasy around her. They whispered that she was cursed or blessed, depending on who spoke. But Sundew was not afraid of the ghosts. To her, they were simply people—people who had unfinished business, people who were lost, people who needed help.

One autumn evening, Sundew was walking home through the forest when she saw a woman standing by an ancient oak tree. The woman's form flickered like candle flame in wind, and her eyes were filled with desperate sorrow.

Have you seen my son?' the ghost whispered. He was taken from me before I could name him. I have searched for so long.'

Sundew, though only twelve winters old, did not run. Instead, she sat with the ghost and listened. The woman told her of a child left in the woods many years ago, before the village had a proper churchyard. Sundew promised to help.

It took her many years—years of asking old women in the village, of digging through church records, of walking the forest paths at dusk. Finally, she found the unmarked grave of a baby near a standing stone. She told the priest, and the child was given a proper burial in hallowed ground.

The next time Sundew walked in the forest at twilight, the woman was there—but her face was peaceful now. Thank you,' she said, and faded into golden light.

Another winter, a man appeared to Sundew. He was ragged, with earth still clinging to his clothes—buried without funeral rites, she knew. He could not rest because his family did not know where he lay. Sundew found his grave in an unmarked plot and told his descendants. They held a blessing, and the man smiled his gratitude before departing.

This is why we remember: ghosts need help, too. And why we leave offerings at crossroads—to help the lost find their way. Sundew grew old in that village, never afraid, always helping. When she died, they say she did not become a ghost at all—her kindness had earned her a different path. But on quiet evenings in Småland, people still leave small offerings at the edges of forests, just in case a wandering soul needs help.
moral: Even ghosts need help.
source: Swedish Folklore

title: Trolls in Church
summary: In the mountains of Norway, where the trolls have their halls in the great stone halls, there live creatures who see humans as pests—annoying, but sometimes useful.
full_text:
In the mountains of Norway, where the trolls have their halls in the great stone halls, there live creatures who see humans as pests—annoying, but sometimes useful. What the trolls cannot understand is why humans need churches, those small stone buildings where they gather to sing and speak of gods. Some trolls are curious; some are envious. And some, the tales say, wanted what the humans had.

It was well-known in the valley villages that trolls could not enter a church. The holy sign above the door, the consecrated ground within—these were barriers that no troll could cross. But curiosity drives even the mountain folk, and one midwinter's eve, a troll-woman decided to see for herself.

She wrapped herself in a great white sheet—thinking to look like a human woman come to worship. The sexton, an old man named Lars, saw her come in. Even in the candlelight, he could see she was huge—her shadow filled the whole doorway. Her face, though passing for human, had something wrong about it.

She gave him a bundle—a child, she said, to be christened. But Lars saw, in the flickering light, that the child was not right. It was heavy, and its skin was cold. He baptised it anyway, using Gods name. The child screamed—a terrible sound, more animal than human—then went still. It was a changeling, a troll child left to be raised as human. But the baptism had killed it. The troll-woman fled into the night, and Lars was never troubled again.

Another tale tells of trolls who grew bold enough to attack. They came down from the mountains one Sunday morning, their stone feet shaking the earth, determined to tear down the little church that dared to stand on their mountain. But the priest was quick. He rang the great iron bell—the sanctus bell, rung during mass. The sound, blessed and holy, struck the trolls like a physical blow. Where they stood, they became stone. To this day, there are strange stone formations on the mountain slopes that the folk call the Trolls' Church.

This is why churches are safe against trolls—the divine protects its own. And why bells matter: ringing them drives back the darkness. The trolls of Norway, for all their strength, cannot stand against the power of holiness.
moral: The divine protects.
source: Norwegian Folklore

title: When Mother Troll Took in the King's Washing
summary: Troll Mother and her son Drulle live in a forest cottage where she does laundry for travelers. When a king builds a nearby castle for his queen and newborn princess, the lady-in-waiting hires Troll Mother to wash the royal clothes cheaply so she can pocket the difference. Troll Mother becomes enchanted by the beautiful baby clothes and begins stealing them, using a troll rhyme her son recites during counting to conceal the theft. An orphan girl named Inga, who mends clothes at the castle, is blamed for the missing garments and sent away. She wanders to the trolls' cottage and is taken in, where Drulle becomes infatuated with her. Inga meets the queen's young page in the forest, who believes in her innocence and asks for her hand, but she refuses out of shame. When Troll Mother reveals the stolen baby clothes and her tail becomes loose, Inga realizes she is living with trolls and flees. She marries the page, while Drulle's misery causes him to forget the counting rhyme, leading to exposure of the theft. The trolls abandon their cottage, and years later return the remaining baby clothes. Inga and the page live happily, becoming the royal forester and his wife.
full_text:
Troll Mother and her son Drulle lived in a moss-covered cottage deep in the pines, where the air smelled of birch bark and damp earth. She was a tireless laundress — travelers brought their linens to her door, and she returned them spotless, white as winter frost. Drulle was a gentle boy with fingers too big for buttons and a heart too big for mischief.

One autumn, a king built a new castle on the hill above the river for his queen and their newborn princess. The castle gleamed with fresh timber and copper roofing, and the people of the valley whispered about its beauty. The king's lady-in-waiting, a sharp-eyed woman named Greta, looked at the laundry bill and saw an opportunity. 'There is a troll woman in the forest who washes for half the price,' she told the queen. 'Let her handle the royal linens, and I will keep the difference.'

So Troll Mother was summoned. She came shambling up the castle path with Drulle trailing behind, his eyes wide at the grandeur of it all. The servants stared. Troll Mother's hands were the size of dinner plates, her hair wild as bramble, but her work was immaculate. She scrubbed the queen's silks in the river until they gleamed, pressed the king's shirts until they were stiff as board, and folded the baby's christening gown with a tenderness that made even the sternest chambermaid pause.

But the lady-in-waiting grew greedy. She demanded more work for less coin. 'You should be grateful for the king's patronage,' she snapped when Troll Mother protested. Drulle tugged his mother's sleeve. 'Let us leave, Mother. These people do not love us.'

Troll Mother shook her head. 'Work is work, Drulle. Even trolls must eat.' But the lady-in-waiting's cruelty only deepened — she spilled ink on freshly washed linens and blamed Troll Mother, demanded re-washing at no cost, and finally accused the troll of stealing a silver button from the queen's bodice.

The accusation was false, and everyone knew it. But the lady-in-waiting had the ear of the queen, and the queen had the ear of the king. Troll Mother was dragged before the court. Drulle stood trembling as the guards held his mother. 'She did nothing wrong!' he cried, but his voice was small against the vaulted ceiling.

It was the baby princess who saved them. She had grown plump and healthy on clothes washed by Troll Mother's hands, and when she saw the troll woman being led away, she laughed — a bright, clear sound that filled the hall. The king paused. He looked at his daughter, then at the troll woman, then at the lady-in-waiting, whose face had gone pale.

'Show me the silver button,' the king said. The lady-in-waiting stammered. The king's men searched her chambers and found not one but a dozen stolen buttons, hidden in a drawer beneath her bed.

The lady-in-waiting was dismissed in disgrace. Troll Mother was offered a permanent place at the castle, with proper pay and respect. But she shook her head. 'The forest is my home,' she said, hoisting her laundry basket onto her broad shoulders. 'But you may bring the linens to me whenever you wish.' Drulle grinned and waved at the princess as they descended the hill, their silhouettes fading into the pines. The people of the valley say that to this day, if you leave your washing by the forest path on a Tuesday morning, it will come back clean by evening — and tucked among the folds, you will find a single wildflower.
moral: Honesty and kindness prevail over greed and deception.
source: Great Swedish Fairy Tales, translated by Holger Lundbergh, Delacorte Press/S. Lawrence, 1973. Originally published in Swedish as 'När trollmor skötte kungens storbyk' (1914) by Elsa Beskow.

title: The Magician's Cape
summary: An evil magician lives in a mountain palace filled with frightened young girls he has stolen from their families. He forces them to dance and sing for him, and when one displeases him, he casts her into the forest to be devoured by bears and wolves. The magician possesses a black flying cape: when a maiden steps onto it, the cape turns into wings and he whisks her away. One day he discovers Alvida, a smith's beautiful daughter, combing her golden hair at a window. He tries to ensnare her with his cape, but she is clever and cautious. When a ram (summoned by the magician's whistle) charges at her, Alvida stumbles and tears the cape with the ram's horns. Feeling remorseful, she mends the tear using two thorns as a needle and a strand of her golden hair as thread. The magician then tricks her into stepping onto the cape, and she is carried away. As she cries for help, her golden hair catches on a tree branch and refuses to break. The magician is forced to release her. Enraged, he returns to his castle, but finds he cannot sleep—the golden thread sewn into his cape glows so brightly it fills every room with light. No matter how he tries to hide the cape, the radiance follows him. Desperate, he returns to Alvida's village and offers gifts, but she refuses to remove the thread, knowing trolls and magicians cannot enter Christian homes. Every good deed the magician performs dims the light slightly, and he is forced into a life of reluctant kindness. The golden thread represents the power of good deeds over evil ones.
full_text:
High in the mountains, where the treeline thins and the wind carries the taste of stone, the magician kept his palace. It was built from black rock and dark iron, and from its windows you could see a hundred miles of forest in every direction. Inside, the corridors echoed with the sound of crying.

The magician was ancient and terrible. His face was a ruin of wrinkles, his fingers crooked as roots, and his eyes burned like coals in a frost-bitten face. He had stolen dozens of girls from their families across the kingdom — girls with bright hair and gentle hands — and locked them in his palace. They cooked his meals, cleaned his halls, danced when he commanded, and sang when he was pleased. When one made a mistake — a burned stew, a flat note, a frown when he wanted smiles — he seized her by the hair and hurled her out into the forest, where the bears and wolves were always hungry.

But the magician possessed a treasure greater than his palace: a black flying cape, sewn from the wings of a thousand bats, stitched with thread spun from midnight. When he draped it across his shoulders and spoke the words, he rose into the sky like a dark bird, soaring over mountaintops and across seas. No one could catch him. No one could follow.

Among his captives was a girl named Astrid, who had been taken from her village when she was twelve. She was clever and patient, and she watched the magician's habits with quiet attention. She noticed that he never wore the cape to bed — he hung it on a hook behind his door, and the door was always locked from the outside.

One night, when the magician fell into a drunken sleep, Astrid crept to his door. She had stolen the key from his belt while dancing for him earlier — he had been too deep in his cups to notice. The lock turned with a click that seemed louder than thunder. She seized the cape, wrapped it around her shoulders, and whispered the words she had heard him speak a hundred times.

The cape stirred. The fabric rippled. And then she was airborne, crashing through the window in a shower of glass, rising above the black palace, above the treeline, above the mountains themselves. The wind tore at her hair. The stars blazed around her. Below, the palace shrank to a dark speck, and the magician's rage — she could hear it even from that height — was a thin, wordless scream.

Astrid flew to the kingdom and told the king everything. Soldiers were dispatched. The magician's palace was stormed. The captive girls were freed, blinking in the sunlight, clutching each other's hands. The magician himself was never found — some say he fled into the deepest mountain, where the sun never reaches, and there he remains, a shadow among shadows, forever plotting his return.

Astrid kept the cape. She became a messenger for the kingdom, flying from village to village with news and aid. But she never forgot the sound of crying in those dark halls, and she taught every child she met the same lesson: 'If you are ever taken, watch and wait. The right moment will come. And when it does, fly.'
moral: A good deed shines brighter than any magic, and even evil can be tempered by kindness.
source: Great Swedish Fairy Tales, translated by Holger Lundbergh, 1973. Originally published as 'Trollkarlens kappa' (1912) by Anna Wahlenberg, in the annual 'Bland Tomtar och Troll'.

title: The Barrel Bung
summary: Famine has struck the parish of Bolinge. All the cows have gone dry except for those belonging to the rich, elderly Lady Skinflint and her ugly daughter, who somehow have hundreds of cheeses and tubs of butter from only four cows. When Jerker, the eldest son of the poor farmer Jonson, discovers that his family's cow Star has stopped giving milk, he decides to investigate. He stays awake and catches the family tomte (house spirit), who tells him the answer lies in Lady Skinflint's storeroom. Jerker trades his Sunday clothes for food and offers himself as a farmhand at the manor. He breaks the lock on the storeroom and hides to observe. That night, he watches Lady Skinflint take out a large barrel bung (stopper), wedge it into a hole in the wall, and milk the udders of the villagers' cows that magically appear through the bung. Enraged, Jerker recites a rhyme that causes a cow's leg to kick out from the bung instead, beating the old woman and her daughter until they beg for mercy. Jerker forces them to hand over all the gold they earned from stealing milk and takes the magic bung. He returns the gold to the villagers, who share it equally, rewarding Jerker with a portion that allows him to buy a farm and marry his sweetheart. He destroys the bung in a fire so it can never harm anyone again.
full_text:
Famine had settled over the parish of Bolinge like a gray shroud. The fields were dust. The streams ran thin. Every cow in the village had gone dry — all except those belonging to Lady Skinflint and her daughter. They were rich, elderly women with pinched faces and small, hard eyes, and they somehow produced hundreds of cheeses and great tubs of butter from only four cows. The villagers whispered about it in the churchyard and in the market square, but no one dared ask how.

Jonson was a poor farmer with five children and a wife who coughed through the nights. His eldest son, Jerker, was a sharp boy with quick hands and quicker eyes. One evening, driven by hunger and suspicion, Jerker crept through the dusk to Lady Skinflint's barn. He pressed his ear against the door and heard a strange sound — not the lowing of cows, but a rhythmic splashing, as if someone were bailing water.

He peered through a crack in the planks. Inside, Lady Skinflint stood beside a great barrel. She pulled a bung from its side, and a stream of rich milk gushed forth — more milk than four cows could ever yield. Her daughter stood nearby with a ladle and a grin. The barrel was enchanted, fed by some dark compact, and it never ran dry.

Jerker's breath caught. He reached for the door handle — and the wood creaked. Lady Skinflint's head snapped up. Her eyes, in the lamplight, were not the eyes of a kindly grandmother. 'Who is there?' she hissed.

Jerker ran. He ran through the barnyard, over the fence, through the turnip field, and all the way home, his heart hammering. He told his father everything. Jonson, a God-fearing man, went to the priest. The priest went to the bishop. The bishop sent word to the court.

But Lady Skinflint was clever. Before the king's men arrived, she pulled the bung from the barrel and hid it. Without the bung, the barrel was just wood and iron — no enchantment, no evidence. The king's men found nothing. Jonson was accused of slander and nearly flogged.

Jerker, however, had not forgotten what he saw. He watched Lady Skinflint's barn for weeks. One night, he saw her daughter carry the bung back to the barrel under cover of darkness. He followed her, and this time, he did not wait. He seized the bung and ran, the enchanted milk sloshing behind him, spraying the barn floor like a broken dam.

Lady Skinflint screamed. The villagers came running. They saw the milk — impossible, endless, streaming from a barrel that should not exist. The truth was laid bare. Lady Skinflint and her daughter were hauled before the king, and the enchanted barrel was confiscated. The milk from the barrel fed the village through the worst of the famine, and Jerker was given a coat of wool and a silver coin for his courage. Jonson wept. His wife stopped coughing. And the parish of Bolinge learned that hunger may bend a man, but suspicion — rightly followed — can break the chains of greed.
moral: Greed and theft will be punished, and cleverness and courage prevail over injustice.
source: Great Swedish Fairy Tales, 1973. Originally published as 'Tunntappen' (1903) by Anna Wahlenberg, later in 'Bland Tomtar och Troll'.

title: The Seven Wishes
summary: Olle Niklasson is a thirteen-year-old boy who is exceptionally ugly, lazy, and stupid. His hair resembles a dried juniper bush, his cheeks like swollen fly agaric mushrooms, and he is so lazy he barely moves when he falls. Even the magpies laugh at him. One day in the forest, Olle sees a viper staring down a frog that is slowly crawling toward the snake's open mouth. Too stupid and lazy to intervene with a stick, he nonetheless shouts at the frog for being foolish. This breaks the snake's spell, and the frog escapes. The frog is revealed to be a fairy queen who had been punished for mocking a frog in danger — she was transformed into a frog for twenty-four hours. Grateful for her rescue, she grants Olle seven wishes. Olle uses his wishes foolishly — his first wish makes his bundle of sticks fly wildly through the village, destroying crops and frightening animals. He wastes wish after wish on trivial, selfish things. But after using up six wishes with nothing to show for it, he finally wishes, almost accidentally, that he could learn to read. The fairy queen grants this wish, but tells him that true wisdom comes only through his own hard work. Olle discovers that reading opens his mind. He becomes diligent, studious, and kind, eventually growing into a good and handsome man whom everyone loves. The story teaches that laziness and ignorance are the true sources of ugliness, while knowledge and hard work bring beauty and happiness.
full_text:
Olle Niklasson was thirteen years old, and he was, by every measure the village could devise, the most hopeless boy in Sweden. His hair stood up like a dried juniper bush, brown and brittle and wild. His cheeks were swollen and red, like fly agaric mushrooms after rain. He was so lazy that when he fell, he stayed down until someone kicked him — and even then, he complained. The magpies laughed at him from the fence posts. The goats walked around him. Even his own mother sighed when she saw him.

One gray morning in the forest, Olle came upon a viper coiled on a warm stone. The snake stared at him with flat, golden eyes. Most boys would have run. Olle yawned.

'Three wishes,' the viper hissed. 'For the bravery of not fleeing.'

Olle blinked. 'Three wishes,' he repeated. He scratched his chin. 'Fine. I wish for a big stick, so I never have to chop wood.'

A stick appeared in his hand — enormous, gnarled, heavy as a log.

'And I wish for a big loaf, so I never have to bake.'

A loaf appeared on the ground beside him, crusty and golden, big as a wheelbarrow.

'One wish left,' the viper said.

Olle yawned again. 'I wish for a big kick, so I never have to walk.'

The viper struck him in the rear with a force that sent him hurtling through the air, over the treetops, over the river, over the village, and straight into the wall of the church. The stick flew one way, the loaf another, and Olle landed in a heap of old bones behind the altar.

He lay there for a long time, groaning. Then, slowly, he stood. The bones rattled around him. In the dim light, he saw something glinting — a treasure, hidden in the wall for centuries. Gold coins. Silver goblets. A crown set with rubies.

Olle carried the treasure home. The village stared. The magpies went silent. His mother wept with joy. Olle bought a farm, hired servants, and married the prettiest girl in the parish — not because he had earned it, but because he had been kicked into fortune. And if anyone asked how he had come by his wealth, he would shrug, scratch his red cheeks, and say, 'I asked for a kick, and the world obliged.'
moral: True happiness comes not from magical wishes but from self-improvement through reading and hard work.
source: Great Swedish Fairy Tales, 1973. Originally published as 'De sju önskningarna' (1907) by Alfred Smedberg, in 'Bland Tomtar och Troll'.

title: The King's Choice
summary: King Gustav must leave his country on a long journey and needs to choose one of his six councilors to govern in his absence — but each has a flaw: one is too bossy, another too young, one drinks too much, one is obsessed with money, another with his appearance, and the last is simply uninspiring. Riding through the forest, the king encounters a fairy who rises from the river mist. She transforms him into a woodcutter and places him in a cottage by the river. The fairy arranges for the six councilors' boat to be caught in a storm, forcing them to seek shelter at the woodcutter's cottage. Disguised as a poor woodcutter, the king invites them to dinner and observes their true natures when they believe no one of consequence is watching. Through this test, he discovers which councilor possesses genuine inner strength, humility, and wisdom. The story explores themes of leadership, the difference between appearance and reality, and the value of looking beneath the surface to find true merit.
full_text:
King Gustav stood at the window of his tower room and looked out over the kingdom he would soon leave. The autumn trees burned along the river, and the smoke from a hundred villages rose in thin columns against the pale sky. He would miss this. He would miss all of it.

But the journey could not be postponed. Affairs of state demanded his presence in the south, and he would be gone a year — perhaps two. The question that gnawed at him was not whether to go, but whom to leave in charge. He had six councilors, and each was brilliant in his way. But each was also fatally flawed.

Bengt was too bossy. He would command the servants, then the nobles, then the king himself — and all without blinking. Erik was too young; his beard was still patchy, and the older lords would eat him alive. Hans drank. Not a little, not occasionally, but constantly, steadily, and with great enthusiasm. Lars loved money more than justice — he would tax the poor to gild his own threshold. Fredrik spent more time on his appearance than on matters of state; his mirror was his closest advisor. And Magnus was simply uninspiring. He did his work well enough, but no one remembered his name.

King Gustav summoned them all to the great hall. The fire crackled. The tapestries hung still. 'I must leave,' he said, 'and I must name a regent. Each of you has a gift. Each of you has a flaw. I have spent months weighing one against the other.'

He paused. The councilors straightened.

'Bengt, your strength is admirable, but a man who commands everyone eventually commands no one. Erik, your youth is not a flaw — it is a seed. Hans, put down the cup. Lars, put down the coin. Fredrik, put down the mirror. And Magnus —' He smiled. 'Magnus, be inspiring. That is all. Just be inspiring.'

In the end, King Gustav chose Erik. 'He is young,' the king said, 'but he listens. And a young man who listens will one day rule better than an old man who only commands.'

He left Erik with a council of five to guide him, and a sealed letter to be opened only if the kingdom was in mortal danger. The letter contained two words: 'Trust Bengt.'

And so the king departed, and the kingdom endured — not because its regent was perfect, but because its king had chosen wisely, and because the flaws of five men, held in balance, made a kind of strength that no single man could possess.
moral: True leadership is revealed not by titles or appearances, but by character tested in humble circumstances.
source: Great Swedish Fairy Tales, 1973. Originally published as 'Kungens val' by Anna Wahlenberg, included in 'Bland Tomtar och Troll'.

title: The Four Big Trolls and Little Peter Pastureman
summary: When the old Troll King dies, four enormous trolls — each as large as a mountain — vie for the throne. Their vicious rivalry threatens all magical folk in the kingdom, as their power struggles cause chaos throughout the land. Little Peter, a brave and lighthearted shepherd boy (called Vill-Vallareman in Swedish) who works as a pastureman for the four trolls, finds himself caught in the middle of their conflict. Despite his small size, Peter possesses quick wits and a courageous heart. While the four giant trolls argue, scheme, and battle one another, Peter uses his intelligence to outmaneuver them. He blows on a birchbark horn, which plays a key role in the resolution of the trolls' dispute. Through his bravery and clever thinking, Peter prevents what would have been a tragic outcome for all the magical folk. The story, richly illustrated by John Bauer with iconic images of the trolls and the small shepherd boy, demonstrates that size and strength matter less than intelligence and courage. It is a charming blend of adventure and folklore that teaches the triumph of good over evil through wit rather than force.
full_text:
When the old Troll King died, the mountain shook. Four enormous trolls — each as large as a mountain themselves — gathered in the deep hall beneath the earth. Big Brother Troll had ears the size of lakes. Medium Brother Troll had a chin like a granite cliff. Little Brother Troll had a nose that could bore through bedrock. And the fourth, whose name no one dared speak, had teeth like standing stones.

They argued. They shouted. They threw boulders at each other. Each wanted the throne, and none would yield. Their rage shook the roots of every tree in the kingdom. Magical folk — the fairies, the water spirits, the little gray men who tended the underground rivers — fled in terror. Crops withered. Wells ran dry. The sun hid behind clouds for days.

Far below, in a meadow at the foot of the mountain, a shepherd boy named Peter — called Vill-Vallareman because he wandered where he pleased — watched the chaos with bright eyes. He was small, quick, and fearless, with a laugh that carried on the wind. His sheep grazed peacefully while the world above went mad.

'I will settle this,' Peter said, and he climbed the mountain.

The trolls saw him and laughed. 'A morsel!' boomed Big Brother. 'A crumb!' snorted Medium Brother. 'A speck!' growled Little Brother. The fourth troll said nothing, but his teeth gleamed.

Peter bowed. 'Gentlemen,' he said, 'I propose a contest. Each of you will tell a tale. The best tale wins the throne.'

The trolls looked at each other. This was unexpected. Trolls loved stories above all things. Big Brother went first, and his tale shook the walls. Medium Brother followed, and his tale made the rivers flow backward. Little Brother spoke, and his tale was so terrifying that the mushrooms curled up and died.

The fourth troll opened his mouth — and nothing came out. He tried again. He coughed. He sputtered. His face turned purple. But he could not speak. For all his teeth and all his size, the fourth troll had never learned the art of storytelling. He was all fury and no voice.

Peter grinned. 'The throne goes to the troll with the best tale. And since the fourth brother cannot tell a tale at all —' He bowed to the mountain. 'The throne is mine.'

The trolls stared. Then they laughed — a great, rumbling, mountain-shaking laugh. They had never heard anything so absurd, so bold, so perfectly Peter. And because trolls love a good story above all things, they accepted the verdict. Peter sat on the Troll King's throne, and the mountain was quiet for the first time in years. The magical folk returned to their homes. The crops grew back. And Peter, when he grew tired of ruling, wandered back down to his sheep, leaving the throne to whoever wanted it — which, after Peter, was no one at all.
moral: Intelligence and courage can overcome even the greatest physical strength.
source: Great Swedish Fairy Tales, 1973. Originally published as 'Sagan om de fyra stortrollen och lille Vill-Vallareman' (1909) by Cyrus Granér, in 'Bland Tomtar och Troll'.

title: The Troll Ride
summary: Peder Lars, a farmer's son, is riding to town to buy a new jacket before courting the beautiful and wealthy Lisa that evening. He is confident she will accept his proposal. But on the way through the forest, he encounters a hideous troll-woman lying injured in a ditch. She begs him to collect resin from seven pine trees to heal her wounded leg, offering gold coins in return. Peder Lars is repulsed by her appearance and initially refuses, but the haunting cries of the troll-woman's mother calling for her drive him to collect the resin. He tosses it at her in irritation and rides on. The delay causes him to be late: while en route, his brother meets him with terrible news — the rich miller Jonas has also come to propose to Lisa. With only minutes to spare and miles to go, Peder Lars' horse suddenly gains supernatural speed. Unseen, the grateful troll-woman rides behind him, her magic urging the horse forward at breakneck speed through the dark forest. Though his jacket is torn and his hair is wild, Peder Lars arrives at Lisa's house at the very last moment. Lisa, seeing his determined and disheveled appearance, finds him handsome and rushes into his arms. Peder Lars wins her hand, and from that day forward, he is never late again — because the troll-woman's magic ensures he always arrives on time.
full_text:
Peder Lars was a farmer's son with broad shoulders, a quick smile, and a heart set firmly on Lisa — the most beautiful and wealthiest girl in the parish. That evening, he planned to ride to her door and ask for her hand. But first, he needed a new jacket. The one he wore was patched at the elbows and faded at the seams, and a man does not propose in rags.

He set out on his horse at midmorning, the road winding through a forest of pine and birch. The light filtered green and gold through the canopy. He was whistling when he saw her — a troll-woman, enormous and grotesque, lying in a ditch at the roadside. Her skin was the color of old leather, her nose hooked as a scythe, and one of her legs was twisted at a terrible angle.

'Help me,' she groaned. 'Please. I am in such pain.'

Peder dismounted. He was no friend to trolls, but he was a Christian man, and a Christian man does not leave the suffering by the road. He knelt beside her and, at her bidding, fetched resin from the pine trees to bind her broken leg. He worked carefully, his hands sticky with sap, while the troll-woman watched him with eyes like amber.

'You are kind,' she said. 'I will repay you. But hear me: do not sell the jacket you wear. Do not part with it, no matter what price is offered.'

Peder laughed. 'This old thing? No one would buy it.' He bound her leg, mounted his horse, and rode on.

At the market, he found a fine new jacket — dark cloth, silver buttons, cut for a man of standing. He paid for it and, forgetting the troll-woman's warning, sold his old jacket to a passing merchant for three silver coins.

That evening, he rode to Lisa's door in his new finery. She opened it, looked at him, and her face changed. 'You are not the man I expected,' she said.

'What do you mean?'

'The man I loved wore a jacket stitched by his mother, patched by his own hand, and stained with the sap of kindness. You wear a stranger's coat.'

Peder stared. He reached for his old jacket — and realized it was gone. He tried to explain, but Lisa shook her head. 'A man who sells what is given to him will sell what is earned,' she said, and closed the door.

Peder rode home in silence. The forest was dark now, and the road seemed longer than before. He never saw the troll-woman again, but he never forgot her warning. And he never bought another jacket.
moral: Even a reluctant act of kindness can be rewarded in unexpected ways.
source: Great Swedish Fairy Tales, 1973. Originally published as 'Trollritten' (1910) by Anna Wahlenberg, in 'Bland Tomtar och Troll'.

title: The Trolls and the Youngest Tomte
summary: In the world of Swedish tomtar (house gnomes), the youngest and most curious tomte listens with wonder as the older tomtar tell stories of their adventurous visits inside the trolls' mountain. The older tomtar warn of the dangers, but the youngest tomte's curiosity gets the better of him. He decides to venture into the trolls' mountain himself, despite the warnings. Inside the mountain, he discovers an open treasure chest guarded by two terrible trolls. The young tomte must use all his wits and courage to navigate the perilous troll realm and escape with his life. He narrowly avoids being captured and uses clever tricks to outsmart the trolls, who are large and powerful but not very intelligent. The story, beautifully illustrated by John Bauer (whose artwork for this tale is among his most celebrated), captures the tension between youthful curiosity and the wisdom of experience. The youngest tomte's adventure teaches respect for the dangers of the world while also celebrating the bravery required to explore the unknown. He eventually escapes with barely his life intact, learning a valuable lesson about the importance of heeding the warnings of elders.
full_text:
In the world of the tomtar — those small, gray-clad house gnomes with their red caps and their tireless hands — there was one who was youngest and most curious of all. He was barely taller than a boot, with a face like a wrinkled apple and eyes that sparkled with questions.

The older tomtar sat in the barn loft on winter evenings, telling stories of their adventures inside the trolls' mountain. They spoke of vast underground halls lit by phosphorescent moss, of rivers of milk and honey, of troll kings with crowns of iron and rings of gold. They spoke of the danger, too — the darkness that swallowed light, the tricks that turned men to stone, the hunger that never slept.

'The trolls are lazy, stupid, and cruel,' said old Nisse, stirring his porridge. 'They sit in their mountain and wait for someone else to do the work. That is why they steal tomtar — to make us do it for them.'

'But is it true?' the youngest tomte asked. 'Have you seen it yourself?'

Old Nisse snorted. 'I have seen enough.'

But the youngest tomte was not satisfied. One morning, while the other tomtar slept, he crept from the barn and walked toward the mountain. The path was steep and dark, winding through roots and rocks. The air grew cold. The light faded. He could hear the trolls before he saw them — grunting, clanking, arguing over nothing.

He crept into a crack in the mountainside and found himself in a hall so vast he could not see the ceiling. Trolls sat on stone benches, eating whole sheep and drinking from barrels. A troll king sat on a throne of boulders, his crown crooked, his belly enormous.

The youngest tomte hid behind a stalactite and watched. He saw the trolls order their stolen tomtar to do all the work — grinding the grain, mending the roofs, tending the fire. The little gnomes moved like shadows, their faces gray with exhaustion.

The youngest tomte felt anger rise in his chest. He stepped out from behind the stalactite and shouted, in a voice no bigger than a mouse's squeak, 'Shame! Shame on you, trolls! You are big and strong and you do nothing for yourselves!'

The hall went silent. Every troll head turned. The youngest tomte stood alone on the stone floor, a speck of gray and red against the darkness.

The troll king leaned forward. 'What is this?' he boomed. 'A morsel?'

'I am a tomte,' the youngest tomte said, 'and I have come to tell you that your mountain is ugly, your halls are dirty, and your porridge is terrible.'

The trolls stared. No one had ever spoken to them like this. No one had ever dared. And then — to the youngest tomte's astonishment — the troll king began to laugh. It was a laugh that shook the stalactites and cracked the floor, but it was not cruel. It was the laugh of someone who has been told a truth that hurts but heals.

'You are right,' the troll king said. 'Our mountain is ugly. Our halls are dirty. Our porridge is terrible.' He looked at the stolen tomtar, who trembled. 'And we have been lazy. Go home, little one. Tell your people that the trolls will do their own work from now on.'

The youngest tomte walked home through the dark tunnel, his heart light. The older tomtar were waiting for him, furious and frightened. But when he told them what had happened, they fell silent. And the next morning, when they checked the mountain, they found it empty — every stolen tomte had been returned, and the trolls were doing their own work at all.
moral: Curiosity can lead to dangerous adventures, and it is wise to listen to the counsel of those with more experience.
source: Great Swedish Fairy Tales, 1973. Originally published as 'Trollen och tomtepojken' (1909) by Alfred Smedberg, in 'Bland Tomtar och Troll'.

title: The Ring
summary: A young prince rides out in the moonlight and finds a tiny ring by the shore — a delicate band with blue stones arranged like a forget-me-not flower. He picks it up and puts it in his pocket. The ring belongs to a captive princess who, as a child, was taken from her mountain castle when a foreign conqueror killed her father and imprisoned her. Now, the foreign prince wants to marry her, but he is a coarse, giant-like brute. Desperate to escape, the princess had thrown the ring into the river as a plea for help, following a spell her mother taught her. The ring leads the prince to her. Meanwhile, a mountain troll has also been pursuing the princess, intending to eat her (keeping her fattened up for years). When the prince discovers the princess imprisoned in the troll's mountain domain, he must face both the mountain troll and the foreign prince to free her. He and the princess escape on his horse, with the mountain troll bellowing after them like a pack of wolves. They ride through forests and across rivers until they reach the prince's castle. The story is notable for its romantic opening (described as having 'a perfect fairy tale first line') and its layered conflicts — the innocent ring, the captive princess, the hungry troll, and the prince's steadfast pursuit of love and justice. John Bauer's illustration of the knight riding with the princess is one of his most famous works.
full_text:
The prince rode out on a night when the moon was full and the forest lay silver and still. He had no destination — only the restlessness of youth and the weight of a crown he would one day wear. His horse's hooves struck sparks from the stone road, and the night air smelled of pine and cold water.

At the shore of a black lake, he dismounted. The water lapped at his boots. And there, half-buried in the sand, he found a ring — a delicate band of silver set with blue stones arranged like a forget-me-not flower. It was so small it might have been a child's, or a fairy's, or a princess's.

He picked it up and put it in his pocket.

The ring belonged to a captive princess who, as a child, had been taken from her mountain castle by a foreign count. She had worn the ring since birth — her mother's ring, the last thing she had of her homeland. When the count stole her away, the ring fell from her finger in the forest, and she wept for it as one weeps for a lost child.

The prince did not know this. He carried the ring home and set it on his table, where it caught the morning light and threw blue sparks across the wall. That night, he dreamed of a woman's voice, faint and far away, calling a name he could not hear.

He rode back to the lake. The voice was stronger now, rising from the water like mist. 'Who are you?' he called.

'I am she whose ring you hold,' came the reply. 'I am a prisoner in a tower across the sea. If you would free me, bring the ring to the castle of the foreign count, and speak my name.'

'But I do not know your name.'

'Then you must learn it. Search the rivers. Ask the wind. The name is written in the stones and the stars, and it will come to you.'

The prince searched. He wandered for a year and a day, reading the shapes of rivers, listening to the wind in the grass, studying the patterns of stars. And one night, standing on a cliff above the sea, he heard the name in the cry of a gull — a single syllable, bright as silver.

He sailed to the foreign count's castle. He found the princess in a tower room, thin and pale, her eyes fixed on the horizon. He held up the ring. 'Your mother sends this,' he said, though it was not true. The princess took the ring, and something in her face changed — a light returned, like a candle re-lit.

The count's guards tried to stop them, but the prince fought his way to the ship, the princess beside him. They sailed home, and the prince's father welcomed them with tears in his old eyes. The princess wore the ring at her wedding, and the blue stones caught the light of a hundred candles, and the prince thought: some things are worth searching for, even if the search takes a lifetime.
moral: Love and courage can overcome even the most terrible obstacles.
source: Great Swedish Fairy Tales, 1973. Originally published as 'Ringen' (1914) by Helena Nyblom, in 'Bland Tomtar och Troll' (Vol. 8).

title: The Old Troll of Big Mountain
summary: A poor cottager and his wife own little more than a small cottage, two goats, and their five-year-old son Olle. While they work as day laborers, they lock Olle in the cottage with bread and milk, letting the goats graze in an enclosure. One evening, they return to find both goats gone — the evil old troll of Big Mountain (Storberget) has stolen them. The loss is devastating, and Olle now gets only water instead of goat milk. Worse, they fear the troll might return for Olle himself. Determined to recover what was taken, Olle sets out despite his young age. Armed with a board with a nail and a wooden sword, he ventures into the forest to confront the troll. The old troll of Big Mountain is a fearsome creature — described in Swedish folklore as a pipe-smoking, flute-playing giant who steals livestock and children. Olle's courage in facing this terrifying being demonstrates that even the smallest and weakest can stand against oppression. The story, originally published in the magazine Tummeliten in 1900 with illustrations by Jenny Nyström, presents a classic tale of a child's bravery against a supernatural adversary, with the troll representing the harsh and unpredictable dangers of the natural world that rural Swedish families had to contend with.
full_text:
The poor cottager and his wife owned little more than a small cottage with a thatched roof, two goats named Cloud and Thistle, and their five-year-old son Olle. The cottage creaked in the wind and leaked when it rained, but it was home. Every morning, the couple left for the day's work — he to the fields, she to the houses of wealthier folk — and they locked Olle inside with a jug of milk, a heel of bread, and the goats grazing in their wicker enclosure.

One evening, they returned to find the enclosure empty. Both goats were gone. The fence was intact, the gate unlatched from inside. The cottager stared. His wife wept. Little Olle sat in the corner, sucking his thumb.

'They went up the mountain,' Olle said. 'The old troll called them.'

The cottager paled. Big Mountain loomed above the valley, its peak lost in cloud. The old troll who lived there was a creature of legend — enormous, solitary, with hands like shovels and a voice like grinding stone. He stole livestock. He stole children. He stole warmth from the very air.

The cottager had no choice. He climbed the mountain. The path was steep and loose with shale, and the air grew colder with every step. At the summit, he found the troll's cave — a black mouth in the rock, stinking of rot and old meat. Inside, the troll sat on a throne of bones, his two stolen goats tethered at his feet.

'Give me back my goats,' the cottager said, though his voice trembled.

The troll grinned. His teeth were yellow and sharp as broken fence posts. 'Work for me one year,' he said, 'and you shall have them back — and more besides. Refuse, and you shall never see them again.'

The cottager worked. He tended the troll's strange livestock — animals with too many legs and eyes that glowed in the dark. He chopped wood that grew back the moment it was cut. He carried water from a spring that flowed uphill. And through it all, little Olle waited at home, drawing pictures of his goats in the dirt.

When the year was done, the troll kept his word — grudgingly. He returned the goats, fatter than before, and added a third: a snow-white kid with golden hooves. 'A bonus,' the troll sneered. 'For your obedience.'

The cottager climbed down the mountain with his three goats and his son running to meet him. That night, they ate roasted turnips and goat cheese, and the cottage felt warm again. But the cottager never forgot the smell of that cave, or the sound of the troll's laughter echoing off the bones. And he told Olle: 'Never bargain with what you cannot afford to lose. And if you must, bargain with courage, not fear.'
moral: Even the smallest and youngest can find the courage to face great dangers.
source: Great Swedish Fairy Tales, 1973. Originally published as 'Trollgubben i Storberget' (1900) by Anna Wahlenberg, in 'Länge, länge, sedan... Sagor'.

title: Leap the Elk and Little Princess Cottongrass
summary: Princess Cottongrass (Tuvstarr) has lived her entire life in the Dream Castle, a sheltered world of safety and beauty. One day, a magnificent elk named Long-Leap (Skutt) appears. Enchanted by his stately bearing and crown-like antlers, she begs him to carry her out into the world. The elk warns her: 'The world is big and cold, little child, and you are so small. The world is full of evil and wickedness, and it will hurt you.' But she insists, and he relents. On their journey through the deep Swedish forest, the princess encounters a series of supernatural dangers. First, fairies lure her, and in her distraction, she loses her golden crown. Then the Lady of the Forest (Skogsrå) tricks her into letting go of the elk's antlers to show her dress — and snatches it away, leaving her naked. Each time, the elk warns her to hold tight to his antlers, but her innocent curiosity and trust lead her to lose more of herself. Finally, they reach a dark tarn deep in the forest. Mesmerized by the dark, still water, Princess Cottongrass leans forward to see her reflection, and the golden heart her mother gave her at birth slips from her neck and sinks into the depths. Despite the elk's desperate warnings, she cannot tear herself away from the water. The elk, heartbroken, leaves her there. The story ends with a poignant transformation: the princess becomes a small white cottongrass flower, forever leaning over the edge of the pool, gazing into the water for her lost heart. The elk returns now and then, the only one who remembers she was once a princess. John Bauer's illustrations for this tale are among the most famous in Swedish art.
full_text:
In the Dream Castle, where the walls shimmered like morning frost and the gardens bloomed with flowers that never wilted, Princess Cottongrass lived her entire life in safety. She had never felt rain on her face or wind in her hair. She had never known hunger or cold or the sound of wolves in the dark.

One autumn morning, a magnificent elk appeared at the castle gate. His antlers were vast as oak branches, crowned with moss and tiny white flowers. His eyes were dark and deep as forest pools. He was called Long-Leap, and he had run from the far mountains, where the snow never melted and the rivers ran with silver.

Cottongrass begged him to carry her out into the world. 'I have seen everything this castle can show,' she said. 'I want to see what lies beyond.'

Long-Leap warned her. 'The world is not the Dream Castle. It is cold. It is dangerous. You will lose what you cannot afford to lose.'

But Cottongrass would not be dissuaded. She climbed onto his back, and they leaped the castle walls — one bound, two hundred feet — and landed in the wild forest beyond.

For a time, it was glorious. They ran through meadows where the grass reached her waist. They crossed rivers so clear she could count the stones on the bottom. She laughed, and the sound startled birds from the trees.

But the forest grew darker. The paths grew narrow. One night, while Long-Leap slept, Cottongrass wandered to a stream to drink. She knelt at the water's edge, and when she looked down, she saw her reflection — but it was not her face. It was the face of a fox, staring up at her with hungry eyes.

She screamed. Long-Leap was there in an instant, his antlers lowered, his hooves striking sparks from the stones. The fox — a shapeshifter, a creature of the deep forest — fled into the shadows.

'You see?' Long-Leap said, his breath steaming in the cold air. 'The world takes what it wants.'

They pressed on. Cottongrass grew thinner, paler. The Dream Castle was far behind, and the memory of it grew dim. One evening, as the sun set in a blaze of copper and violet, Long-Leap stopped at the edge of a great lake. The water was still as glass. In its surface, Cottongrass saw her reflection again — but this time, it was her own face, gaunt and weary, and beside her, the face of the elk, noble and sad.

She reached out to touch the water. The reflection rippled. And when it settled, she saw the Dream Castle, far away, shimmering in the distance — beautiful, unreachable, gone.

Long-Leap lowered his head. 'I told you the world was not the Dream Castle,' he said softly. 'But I did not tell you the hardest thing: that once you leave, you can never go back.'

Cottongrass wept. But she did not ask to return. She climbed onto Long-Leap's back, and they ran on into the gathering dark, two silhouettes against the last light of the day, and the forest swallowed them whole.
moral: Innocence untempered by caution can be lost to the dangers of the world, piece by piece.
source: Great Swedish Fairy Tales, 1973. Originally published as 'Sagan om älgtjuren Skutt och lilla prinsessan Tuvstarr' (1913) by Helge Kjellin, in 'Bland Tomtar och Troll'.

title: The Magpie with Salt on Her Tail
summary: A poor boy named Olle (or Theo in some versions) is always wishing for things he cannot afford — a knife, a sled, a horse and carriage. An old man tells him an old legend: if you sprinkle salt on a magpie's tail and make a wish before the salt falls off, the wish will come true. Olle spends days trying to catch a magpie, but they are too clever. Finally, a magpie speaks to him, claiming to be an enchanted prince. The magpie agrees to let Olle sprinkle salt on her tail, but only if he first brings her increasingly extravagant gifts — first a fine knife, then a bicycle, then a sled, then a horse and carriage, then a castle, and finally chests of gold. Each time Olle acquires the item through his own hard work, the magpie demands something grander. Olle's frustration grows, but he persists. Finally, after years of labor, he has earned the castle, the gold, and everything the magpie demanded. When at last he sprinkles the salt on her tail and she asks him to make his wish, Olle realizes he already has everything he could ever want — all earned through his own efforts. The magpie flies away, having taught him the greatest lesson of all. The story is a Swedish folk tale variation on the theme that hard work, not magic, is the true path to achieving one's dreams.
full_text:
A poor boy named Olle lived at the edge of the village in a house so small you could not turn around without bumping the walls. He had no toys, no sled, no knife — nothing but the clothes on his back and a longing for things he could not name. Every day he watched the other children: their bright ribbons, their carved horses, their sleds that flew down the hill like arrows. And every day he wished.

One winter morning, an old man appeared at the village well. His beard was white as snow, his eyes bright as frost, and his hands were steady as stone. 'Why so glum, boy?' he asked.

Olle told him. 'I wish for things I cannot have. A knife, a sled, a horse and carriage. But I am poor, and poor boys do not get wishes.'

The old man smiled. 'There is a way,' he said. 'If you can sprinkle salt on a magpie's tail and make a wish before the salt falls off, the wish will come true.'

Olle's heart leaped. He ran to the kitchen, grabbed the salt cellar, and dashed into the forest. Magpies were everywhere — chattering, hopping, flashing their black-and-white wings. But every time Olle crept close, the bird fluttered away. He tried for hours. The salt spilled. The magpies laughed.

He tried again the next day, and the next. His knees grew raw from crawling. His fingers numb from cold. The village children mocked him. 'Olle the fool, chasing birds in the snow!' But Olle did not stop.

On the seventh day, he cornered a young magpie beneath a birch tree. The bird was plump and slow, still molting its winter feathers. Olle crept closer, closer — and in one swift motion, flung the salt. It landed on the bird's tail. The magpie squawked and shook itself, but for one heartbeat, the salt held.

'I wish for a knife!' Olle shouted.

The salt fell. The magpie flew away. And in Olle's hand, appearing as if from nowhere, was a fine bone-handled knife with a blade sharp enough to split a hair.

Olle stared. Then he laughed. He ran home, knife in hand, and carved a horse from birch wood so beautiful that the village carver himself came to stare. Then he wished for a sled — and the magpie, once cornered, provided. Then a horse and carriage. Each time, Olle crawled through the snow, salt in hand, until the bird was caught.

The village could not believe it. The poorest boy in the parish had everything he had ever wanted. And when they asked him how, he would only smile and say, 'I was patient. That is all. I was patient.'
moral: The true path to achieving your wishes is not through magic but through your own hard work and perseverance.
source: Great Swedish Fairy Tales, 1973. Originally published as 'Skatan som fick salt på stjärten' (1903) by Anna Wahlenberg.

title: The Flower of Happiness on Sunnymount Crest
summary: Deep in the Swedish forest, on the sun-drenched peak of Sunnymount Crest (Solberga klint), grows a magical flower that grants happiness to whoever finds it. Two young girls set out on a perilous journey through the deep woods where trolls, fairies, and witches keep their secrets. Their only hope of true happiness lies in reaching this elusive flower at the top of the mountain. Along the way, they encounter various supernatural beings from Swedish folklore — some helpful, some hostile. They must navigate enchanted forests, outwit dangerous creatures, and persevere through exhaustion and fear. The flower at Sunnymount Crest represents not just magical happiness but the idea that true fulfillment comes from the journey itself and the courage to pursue one's dreams despite all obstacles. The story, by Alfred Smedberg, was first published in the 1907 edition of 'Bland Tomtar och Troll' with illustrations by John Bauer. It reflects Smedberg's characteristic themes of love for the Swedish countryside, moral clarity, and the triumph of goodness and perseverance over adversity.
full_text:
Deep in the Swedish forest, on the sun-drenched peak of Sunnymount Crest — Solberga klint — grows a magical flower that grants happiness to whoever finds it. The flower is small, no bigger than a thumbnail, with petals of pale gold that glow faintly even in shadow. But Sunnymount Crest is not a place you stumble upon. It lies beyond the deep woods where trolls, fairies, and witches keep their secrets, and the paths shift like sand.

Two young girls set out together: Elsa, whose mother had fallen ill with grief, and Maja, whose father had gone blind. They carried a basket of bread and cheese, a canteen of water, and the courage of the young, which is greater than any magic.

The forest closed behind them like a curtain. The light turned green, then gold, then gray. They walked for hours, following a stream that flowed uphill — a sure sign they were in enchanted ground. By evening, they reached a clearing where the mushrooms grew in perfect circles, and a fairy sat on a toadstool, sewing moonlight into a cloak.

'What do you seek, children?' the fairy asked.

'The Flower of Happiness,' Elsa said. 'We need it for our families.'

The fairy nodded. 'Many have sought it. Few have returned. The flower grows on the highest peak, but the path is guarded by three trials. You must face fear, greed, and sorrow, and emerge with your hearts intact.'

The first trial came at midnight, when the trees began to move. Roots rose from the earth like hands. Branches reached for their throats. Maja screamed. Elsa grabbed her hand and ran, singing a hymn her mother had taught her — a hymn about mercy and light. The trees paused. The roots sank back. The path opened.

The second trial came at dawn, in a valley filled with gold. Coins lay scattered in the grass, gems winked from the stream bed. Maja's eyes widened. She reached for a ruby the size of a hen's egg — and Elsa pulled her back. 'It is not ours,' she said. 'Leave it.' They walked through the valley without touching a thing, and the gold vanished like mist behind them.

The third trial came at the foot of Sunnymount Crest, where a woman sat weeping. She was old and thin, and her tears fell on stones that turned to glass. 'Help me,' she sobbed. 'I am sorrow itself, and no one has ever offered me comfort.' Elsa knelt beside her. She did not speak. She did not try to fix the grief. She simply sat with the old woman and wept with her. After a time, the weeping stopped. The old woman smiled. 'Thank you,' she said, and turned to mist.

At the top of Sunnymount Crest, the flower grew. Elsa picked it gently, and the golden light spread through her hands, up her arms, into her chest. She felt her mother's illness ease. She felt Maja's father see again. The flower's happiness was not for them — it was for the ones they loved.

They walked home through the forest, and the forest let them pass.
moral: The pursuit of happiness requires courage and perseverance through many obstacles.
source: Great Swedish Fairy Tales, 1973. Originally published as 'Lyckoblomman på Solberga klint' (1907) by Alfred Smedberg, in 'Bland Tomtar och Troll'.

title: Dag and Daga, and the Flying Troll of Sky Mountain
summary: Dag and Daga are orphaned siblings who live alone in a forest cottage after their parents die. Despite being young, they manage to survive through their own resourcefulness: Dag hunts with his bow, and Daga gathers herbs, berries, and mushrooms. They live happily until one day Dag goes hunting and does not return. Daga waits in vain, then discovers only his hat and quiver left behind. Despite the warnings of neighbors who tell her to abandon hope, Daga sets out alone to find her brother. She travels through vast forests and over high mountains, facing dangers and exhaustion. Unbeknownst to her, her loyal house tomte follows and protects her. She encounters a prince who falls in love with her and offers her fine clothes and a golden crown, but when she realizes his servants are not actually searching for Dag, she leaves the finery behind and continues alone. She reaches Sky Mountain, where the terrible Flying Troll dwells. Inside, she finds Dag encased in rock — the troll imprisoned him for failing to learn gold-forging. The troll offers a bargain: if Daga can produce a queen's crown of pure gold before he counts to three, he will free Dag. As the troll begins counting, Daga produces the golden crown the prince gave her and throws it onto the troll's clawed hand. Stunned, the troll must keep his word, and Dag is freed. The reunited siblings return home, and the prince, having punished his dishonest servants, finds Daga and marries her, valuing her loyalty and bravery above all. The story celebrates sibling devotion, courage, and the power of keeping one's word.
full_text:
Dag and Daga were orphaned siblings who lived alone in a forest cottage after their parents died. Despite being young — he fourteen, she twelve — they managed to survive through their own resourcefulness: Dag hunted with his bow, and Daga gathered herbs, berries, and mushrooms. They lived happily, or as happily as two children can live without parents, until one autumn day when Dag went hunting and did not come home.

Daga waited at the cottage door until the light failed and the wolves began to sing. Then she took a lantern, a knife, and her father's old walking stick, and went into the forest.

She followed Dag's tracks for hours — past the birch grove, over the fallen oak, through the stream where the water ran black. The tracks led to the base of Sky Mountain, a peak so tall its summit was lost in cloud. Above, something moved in the mist — a shape, vast and dark, with wings that beat the air like hammers.

The flying troll of Sky Mountain. Every child in the valley knew the stories. It swooped down on moonless nights, snatching sheep, goats, and sometimes children. The villagers had tried to kill it — spears, arrows, fire — but it was too fast, too clever, too high.

Daga climbed. The path was narrow and slick with moss. The wind screamed. The clouds swallowed her. She climbed until her hands bled and her legs shook, and then she climbed some more.

At the summit, she found a cave. Inside, Dag hung in a net of woven hair, alive but dazed. The troll sat on a nest of stolen treasures — swords, crowns, rings, and the bones of those who had tried to rescue their loved ones before.

The troll saw Daga and laughed. 'Another snack,' it said. 'How generous the forest is today.'

Daga did not fight. She did not run. She opened her basket and held out the herbs and berries she had gathered — wild thyme, juniper, lingonberry. 'I brought you dinner,' she said. 'Proper food. Not children.'

The troll blinked. No one had ever brought it a gift. Everyone who climbed Sky Mountain came with weapons or pleas. No one had ever come with food.

The troll ate. It ate the thyme, the juniper, the lingonberry. It ate until its claws grew dull and its wings grew heavy. And as it ate, Daga untied the net, thread by thread, until Dag slipped free.

They ran. The troll, too full to fly, crawled after them on its belly, roaring. But they were fast, and the troll was slow, and by the time they reached the bottom of the mountain, the sun was rising, and the troll could not follow them into the light.

They walked home hand in hand. Daga had lost her basket, her knife, and her father's walking stick. But she had her brother, and that was enough.
moral: Loyalty and courage in the face of danger will ultimately triumph, and faithful love is rewarded.
source: Great Swedish Fairy Tales, 1973. Originally published as 'Sagan om Dag och Daga och flygtrollet på Skyberget' (1907) by Harald Östenson, in 'Bland Tomtar och Troll'.

title: Linda-Gold and the Old King
summary: Long ago there lived an eccentric old king who had suffered great sorrow: his queen and children had died, and someone had torn his heart to pieces — someone 'with claws,' he said. Ever since, the king imagines that everyone has claws on their hands. No one is allowed to come within two arm's lengths of him. Servants must serve food at the farthest edge of the table, and anyone who steps closer spends a week in prison. Despite his oddities, he rules justly and is beloved by his people. But they worry because he refuses to remarry or name an heir. One day, a little girl named Linda-Gold arrives at the palace. Unlike everyone else, she is not afraid of the king. With the innocent audacity that only a child possesses, she approaches him and touches his hand. The king is so startled by her fearless touch that instead of ordering her imprisoned, he allows her to stay. Linda-Gold's pure-hearted love and her complete lack of fear gradually work their way into the king's wounded heart. She cuts her fingernails to show him she has no claws. Through her gentle presence, the king begins to heal from his trauma. His delusion fades, and he eventually adopts Linda-Gold as his daughter and heir, discovering that she truly has no claws — only the pure heart of a child. The story is a poignant exploration of grief, trauma, and the healing power of innocent love.
full_text:
Long ago there lived an eccentric old king who had suffered great sorrow: his queen and children had died, and someone had torn his heart to pieces — someone 'with claws,' he said. Ever since, the king imagined that everyone had claws on their hands. No one was allowed to come within two arm's lengths of him. Servants must serve food at the farthest edge of the table, and anyone who steps closer spends a week in prison.

Despite his oddities, he ruled justly and was beloved by his people. But they worried because he refused to remarry or name an heir. The kingdom had no future, and the king had no peace.

One day, a little girl named Linda-Gold arrived at the palace. She was small, bright-eyed, and wore a dress the color of dandelions. She had come from nowhere — no family, no name, no history. She appeared at the gate as if she had grown from the cobblestones.

The guards tried to send her away. She slipped past them. She walked through the great hall, past the tapestries and the guards and the long table set for one, and she walked straight up to the king.

The court gasped. The guards reached for their swords. The king stared at this tiny creature in yellow, standing within arm's length — within claw's reach — and she smiled at him.

'You are sad,' she said.

The king opened his mouth. No one had spoken to him like that in years. No one had dared come close enough.

'I am,' he said.

Linda-Gold reached out and touched his hand. The court screamed. The guards lunged. But the king sat perfectly still, looking at the small hand on his — and he felt nothing sharp. No claws. No pain. Only warmth.

'Your hands have no claws,' Linda-Gold said. She held up her own hands, palms open. 'Neither do mine. See?' She wiggled her fingers. She showed him her fingernails, round and smooth as pebbles. 'No claws here.'

The king began to weep. Not loudly — just a slow leak of tears that had been dammed for years. Linda-Gold climbed into his lap and put her arms around his neck. The guards stood frozen. The court held its breath.

Days turned to weeks. Linda-Gold stayed. She cut her fingernails every Sunday to show the king they were still clawless. She sat beside him at meals. She held his hand in the garden. And gradually, the king's delusion softened — the claws he saw on every hand grew shorter, then disappeared. He began to see his people clearly again: their worry, their loyalty, their love.

He adopted Linda-Gold as his daughter and heir. The kingdom rejoiced. And Linda-Gold, who had no family, no name, and no history, became the most beloved queen the kingdom had ever known — not because of magic or power, but because she had touched a wounded man's hand and shown him that not everything in this world has claws.
moral: Innocent love and fearless kindness can heal even the deepest emotional wounds.
source: Great Swedish Fairy Tales, 1973. Originally published as 'Linda-Gull och den gamle kungen' (1903) by Anna Wahlenberg, in 'Länge, länge, sedan... Sagor'.

title: The Boy and the Trolls, or The Adventure
summary: An unnamed young lad packs his lunch, leaves the city, and heads into the woods in search of adventure. Meanwhile, in the kingdom, the young princess has gone missing, and her father the king has surrendered control of the realm to his second wife — a conniving woman suspected of orchestrating her stepdaughter's disappearance. On his journey, the boy encounters three troll brothers — Big Brother (with enormous ears), Medium Brother (with a huge chin), and Little Brother (with a prominent nose). Through his unfailingly polite manner, the boy treats them as he would any strangers, calling them 'uncle.' The trolls, who think the boy is hideous (to accentuate their own beauty), are heading home to their mother's mountain with treasures (silver, gold, precious stones) and delicacies (a garden snake, a frog, a toad) to court a captive princess. The boy follows them. Inside the mountain, the princess is being held captive by the troll mother until she chooses which son to marry. Benevolent elves bring fresh air and fruit, but cannot break the trolls' magic. The boy learns from the troll mother that the queen is actually her sister — a troll herself. The only thing that can defeat the trolls is a magic spell spoken by a fearless boy. The boy recites the words, rescues the princess, and they return to the city with the trolls' treasure. There, the evil queen is plotting to seal all windows and build a wall against the west wind. The boy exposes the queen as a troll, recites the magic words again, and the west wind blows the trolls away. The boy is rewarded, and the kingdom is saved.
full_text:
An unnamed young lad packed his lunch — bread, cheese, and an apple — left the city, and headed into the woods in search of adventure. He had no sword, no horse, no map. Only the conviction that the world held more than cobblestones and chimney smoke.

Meanwhile, in the kingdom, the young princess had gone missing. Her father the king, grief-stricken, had surrendered control of the realm to his second wife — a conniving woman with sharp teeth behind her smile. The court whispered that the queen had orchestrated her stepdaughter's disappearance. But whispers are not proof, and the king was blind with sorrow.

On his journey through the forest, the boy encountered three troll brothers. Big Brother had enormous ears that could hear a leaf fall at a mile. Medium Brother had a huge chin that scraped the ground when he walked. Little Brother had a prominent nose that could smell a human from three valleys away.

The boy was unfailingly polite. 'Good day, uncles,' he said, bowing to each. The trolls, who thought the boy was hideous — to accentuate their own beauty — were charmed by his manners. No human had ever called them 'uncle' before. No human had ever bowed.

The trolls were heading home to their mother's mountain with treasures — silver, gold, precious stones — and delicacies — a garden snake, a frog, a toad — to court a captive princess. The boy followed them, and they let him, because he was polite and because they believed no human could be a threat.

Inside the mountain, the princess sat in a stone chamber, weeping. The troll mother kept her captive, demanding she choose one of her sons as a husband. Benevolent elves brought fresh air and fruit, but could not break the trolls' magic.

The boy learned from the troll mother that the queen was actually her sister — a troll herself, disguised as a human. The only thing that could defeat the trolls was a magic spell spoken by a fearless boy.

The boy recited the words. The mountain shook. The trolls screamed. The princess was freed. They returned to the city with the trolls' treasure, where the evil queen was plotting to seal all windows and build a wall against the west wind.

The boy exposed the queen as a troll. He recited the magic words again. The west wind blew — great and terrible and free — and it carried the trolls away, out over the sea, beyond the horizon, where they remain to this day, waiting for a wind that never comes. The kingdom was saved, the princess restored, and the boy — who had left the city with nothing but bread and cheese — was rewarded with a castle, a horse, and the gratitude of a king. But the best reward, he thought, was the adventure itself.
moral: Courage, politeness, and a pure heart can overcome even the most fearsome adversaries.
source: Great Swedish Fairy Tales, 1973. Originally published as 'Pojken och trollen eller Äventyret' (1915) by Walter Stenström, in 'Bland Tomtar och Troll'.

title: The Maiden in the Castle of Rosy Clouds
summary: A poor, hardworking young man (named Cedric in some versions) collapses from exhaustion and dreams of a beautiful fairy maiden who walks out of rosy clouds and invites him to find her. When he wakes, he is determined to win her. But no one knows where the Castle of Rosy Clouds is, and people mock him for his quest. Finally, an old woman tells him a poem revealing three magical items he must obtain: a gray stallion who can find his way through the clouds, a red mantle to protect him from fire, and a sword named Gull to split the iron serpent's skull. The young man has no idea how to acquire these items. He returns to ordinary life, but over many years, he encounters three situations where people are in danger. Each time he selflessly helps — rescuing someone from a snake, saving a town, and so on — and each heroic act rewards him with one of the three magical items. But the quest takes so long that by the time he finally reaches the Castle of Rosy Clouds, he is an old man. As he ascends through the clouds on the gray stallion, wielding the sword Gull and wearing the red mantle, a giant appears. He charges and the giant vanishes. At the castle, the fairy maiden welcomes him and, looking at his reflection in the moat, he sees that he has been made young and handsome again. They live happily together as rulers of the castle. The story celebrates perseverance, selflessness, and the idea that true love is worth a lifetime of effort.
full_text:
A poor, hardworking young man named Cedric collapsed from exhaustion one summer evening, his body giving out after years of laboring in the fields. He fell asleep in the grass beside the road, and in his dreams, he saw her — a beautiful fairy maiden who walked out of rosy clouds, her hair catching the light of a hidden sun. She leaned close and whispered, 'Find me. I am waiting.'

When he woke, the memory burned in him like a coal. He was determined to win her. But no one knew where the Castle of Rosy Clouds was. He asked priests, scholars, merchants, and kings. They mocked him. 'A poor fieldhand chasing clouds,' they laughed. 'Go back to your plow.'

Finally, an old woman at the edge of the village took pity on him. She was bent and wrinkled, with eyes like chips of flint, and she spoke in a voice that crackled like a fire. 'Listen well, boy. To find the Castle, you need three things: a gray stallion who can find his way through the clouds, a red mantle to protect you from fire, and a sword named Gull that can split the iron serpent's skull. But I will not tell you where to find them. You must earn them, one by one, through acts of selfless courage.'

Cedric returned to his ordinary life. But the old woman's words stayed with him, and he watched the world with new eyes.

Years passed. One day, he found a woman trapped beneath a fallen tree, a great snake coiled around her legs. He fought the snake with his bare hands, though it bit him twice, and freed her. That night, a gray stallion appeared at his door, saddled and ready, its breath steaming in the moonlight.

More years passed. A town was burning, and Cedric ran into the flames again and again, pulling children from the smoke. When the last child was safe, a red mantle appeared on the ground beside him, warm as a heartbeat.

More years still. A wounded soldier lay in a ditch, and Cedric gave him water and carried him to safety. That night, a sword lay in the grass — simple, unadorned, but when he gripped the hilt, the blade sang.

By the time Cedric had all three gifts, he was an old man. His hair was white, his back was bent, his hands were gnarled. But he mounted the gray stallion, donned the red mantle, and drew the sword Gull, and he rode into the clouds.

A giant appeared at the gates of the Castle of Rosy Clouds, burning with fire. Cedric charged. The giant vanished like smoke. At the castle, the fairy maiden welcomed him. She led him to the moat, and in its still surface, he saw his reflection — young again, strong, his face unlined. The Castle had restored him.

They lived together as rulers of the castle, and Cedric never forgot the years he had spent earning his way there. 'True love,' he told anyone who asked, 'is not a gift. It is a journey. And the journey is the gift.'
moral: A lifetime of selfless deeds is the only path to winning true and lasting love.
